items.attribution: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth' (known as 'The Gospel of Wealth'), North American Review, June 1889
items.exemplar: (a) Carnegie argues that great inequality of wealth is a beneficial result of civilization, and that the important question is how the rich administer — give away — their wealth so that rich and poor remain bound together. (b) It appealed to the middle class because it treated great fortunes as legitimate while insisting the wealthy owed something to society, matching middle-class beliefs in morality and self-improvement without threatening the economic order. (c) Carnegie welcomed inequality as progress; labor leaders argued instead that workers deserved better wages and hours — the AFL under Gompers made those bread-and-butter demands its program, while the Knights of Labor sought broader reforms — and they built unions and strikes to win them.
items.fact_source: PD: Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889 (wording verified against Wikisource original) + u6.md §Key terms — Gospel of Wealth (1889); §The story — Knights of Labor; AFL under Gompers

parts.prompt: Identify Carnegie's main argument about wealth in this passage.
Explain why Carnegie's argument appealed to many middle-class Americans.
Compare Carnegie's view of industrialization with the view held by leaders of the labor movement.

items.stimulus_text: 'The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.... The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.'

items.attribution: Henry W. Grady, 'The New South' speech, New England Society dinner, New York City, December 1886
items.exemplar: (a) Grady wanted the South to move beyond cotton agriculture worked by enslaved labor and build a diversified industrial economy with many small farms. (b) Sharecropping contradicted the 'hundred farms' promise because croppers owned no land and worked under the landowner's direction, giving up half of their crop — they were dependent laborers, not independent farmers. (c) Change: the postwar South gained new industries, railroads, and cities that the antebellum South lacked. Continuity: agriculture — especially cotton — remained central, and Black Southerners remained at the bottom of the labor system, now as sharecroppers and segregated workers rather than enslaved people.
items.fact_source: PD: Grady speech, Dec 1886 + PD: Grimes sharecropping contract, 1882 + u6.md §The story — disenfranchisement constitutions; Plessy v. Ferguson

parts.prompt: Identify Grady's vision for the Southern economy.
Explain one way the sharecropping system contradicted Grady's vision.
Compare the economy of the New South with the economy of the antebellum South, noting one continuity and one change.

items.stimulus_text: 'The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy... a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.'
